title: Volunteering and health
hookLine: volunteers had lower mortality in a review, though healthier people may volunteer more

cards: A clipboard hangs by the door of a food bank. Names, phone numbers, a column for shifts. Saturday, nine to eleven.
One person's handwriting is neat, another's is a scrawl. Sheets like this hang in church halls, animal shelters, libraries and gurdwaras.
Researchers have asked a blunt question about the people who sign them: do they live longer? They found an answer, and then had to qualify it carefully.

teach.b: First, the finding. Morris Okun and colleagues pooled studies of older adults and volunteering in a review in the journal Psychology and Aging.
Across those studies, older people who volunteered had lower death rates over the years they were followed. Second, the catch, and it's a big one.
You have to be fairly well to stand at a food bank for two hours, so healthier people may simply volunteer more.
When the researchers accounted for health and other factors, the gap got smaller, though it didn't vanish: a real link, with the direction still argued over. Third, a word from one tradition.
Sikhs call selfless service seva. In gurdwaras, volunteers cook and serve in the langar, the free kitchen where anyone can sit and eat.
In Sikh teaching, seva is done without looking for a reward, and that includes a health reward. The dal is stirred for the guests, not for anyone's lifespan.
Fourth, Kahlil Gibran's The Prophet, on giving: "You give but little when you give of your possessions. It is when you give of yourself that you truly give." An hour is that kind of gift.
You can't wire it; you have to show up. The science says volunteers tend to do well. The traditions say the point is the person on the other side of the table.

how: Some religious communities organize regular volunteering, from food banks to the Sikh langar, where volunteers cook and serve free meals to anyone who comes.

o: lower death rates in volunteers, with a catch about health
a rule that only religious service counts for health
proof that giving time cures illness in older people

games.q: you're reading the volunteering review. volunteers lived longer. what's the first question an honest researcher asks?
o: "were the volunteers healthier to begin with?"
games.why: you have to be fairly well to volunteer. when health and other factors were accounted for, the gap got smaller but didn't vanish.

practice: Let one face or place come to mind that could use an hour of somebody's time: a neighbor who can't carry groceries, a kitchen that feeds people, a kid who needs a reader, someone alone.
Pass over the most impressive option and settle on the one you would actually do, and roughly when. Hold that person or place in mind for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Volunteering and health. A real link, with a catch: healthier people may volunteer more. And a week ends: cold water, yoga, tai chi, sleep, nature, purpose, service. Seven honest looks. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: seva, selfless service, the word Sikhs use for work like cooking and serving in the langar.

carryVoice: Your line: give an hour. A week of honest looks ends at a table, with someone on the other side. See you tomorrow.
